article.headline: Vidu's 'Reference to Video' Puts Any Face Into Any Scene
article.lede: A Chinese AI video platform called Vidu has released a feature that takes a single still photograph of a person and inserts that likeness into generated video scenes — including scenes with multiple actors. The company's promotional tagline, 'Anyone can be an actor,' captures the ambition plainly. The release has drawn attention from AI observers who see it as a meaningful step toward solving one of generative video's longest-standing problems.
article.body:
The core difficulty in AI-generated video has never been producing plausible motion; it has been keeping a specific person's face consistent across frames, scenes, and lighting conditions. Early text-to-video systems generated new faces freely but could not reliably reproduce the same one twice. **Character consistency** — the ability to anchor a recognizable identity across a clip — has been the gap separating demo reels from practical production tools.

Vidu's 'Reference to Video' feature attacks that gap directly. A user supplies one photograph; the system is supposed to preserve that likeness throughout the generated output, even when placing the subject into unfamiliar environments or alongside other figures. The promotional video for the launch carries the tagline 'Yes, Vidu — Anyone can be an actor,' framing the feature as a democratisation of casting rather than a technical milestone.

The poster, @hq4ai, describes the results as solving character consistency 'almost perfectly' and calls it 'one of the most exciting features I've seen this year.' That enthusiasm is worth contextualising: 'almost perfectly' is a high bar that independent evaluations have not yet confirmed, and promotional footage is by definition curated. Competing platforms — including *Kling AI*, which a separate tutorial explicitly positions Vidu against — have been developing similar identity-anchoring capabilities, so the competitive gap may be narrower than the launch framing suggests.

The model version referenced in the tutorial is **Vidu Q1**, suggesting a versioned product line rather than a one-off experiment. Whether the feature holds up across diverse skin tones, ages, and complex multi-person compositions — conditions that stress-test any face-preservation system — remains an open question from the publicly available evidence.

concepts.definition: In AI video generation, character consistency means the same person's face, build, and distinguishing features remain stable across every frame of a clip. Without it, a generated video of 'you' might drift into a slightly different face mid-scene. Achieving it requires the model to anchor identity from a reference image rather than freely hallucinating each frame.

A generation mode where the user supplies a still image — typically a face photograph — as a constraint on the output video. The model is directed to reproduce that specific likeness within the generated scene, as opposed to text-to-video, where faces are invented from scratch.

A class of AI systems that generate short video clips from written descriptions. They have advanced rapidly since 2023 but have historically struggled to maintain consistent character identity, since each frame is generated with some independence from the others.

article.fact_check: The claim that Vidu's feature solves character consistency 'almost perfectly' is a promotional assertion made by the poster, not an independently verified finding. The evidence presented is a curated promo video — inherently a best-case showcase. Multi-actor scenes and diverse subject conditions are precisely where face-preservation systems tend to degrade, and no third-party benchmark results are cited.
